blocks.prompt: What the Whiskers Are For
blocks.text: A cat has whiskers on its face. It has whiskers over its eyes and under its chin. It even has short whiskers on the back of its front legs. Whiskers are not hairs for warmth. Each whisker sits deep in the skin, and it can feel the tiniest push of air. A cat cannot see well up close. The food in its bowl is a blur. So the cat leans in and lets its whiskers do the looking. In a dark room, whiskers tell the cat where the chair leg is before it bumps into it.

blocks.prompt: The Tongue With Hooks In It
blocks.text: Run your hand along a cat's tongue and it feels like sandpaper. That is not an accident. A cat's tongue is covered in hundreds of tiny spines called papillae. They are made of keratin, the same hard stuff as your fingernails, and every one of them curves backward toward the cat's throat. Those hooks do real work. When a cat eats, they scrape meat off bone. When a cat washes, they rake through fur like a comb and drag out loose hair and dirt. Scientists took a close look at the spines in 2018 and found something nobody expected. Each spine is not a solid point. It is scooped out, like a tiny ladle, and it carries a drop of spit down to the skin at the bottom of the fur. That is why a cat can clean itself so well. The tongue is not just brushing the outside. It is delivering water where the brush cannot reach. The spit dries and cools the cat down too, which matters, because a cat sweats only through its paws. There is one catch. All that raked out fur has to go somewhere, and the hooks point backward, so the cat cannot spit it out. It swallows it. That is where hairballs come from.

answers: papillae
keratin, the same hard stuff as fingernails
they scrape meat off bone and rake loose fur and dirt out
(inference: the hooks point backward, so fur can only travel down the throat)

notes: Tapetum lucidum: a mirror behind the retina
Sees in about one sixth of our light

blocks.prompt: Built for the Dark
blocks.text: A house cat is most awake at dawn and dusk, when the light is thin and the mice are moving. Almost everything about its head is built for that hour. Start with the eyes. Behind a cat's retina sits a layer called the tapetum lucidum, a mirror made of tiny crystals. Light that the retina misses on the way in bounces off that mirror and passes back through for a second chance. Almost nothing is wasted. A cat can see in about one sixth of the light a person needs. The mirror is also why cat eyes flash green in a flashlight beam. You are seeing the light come back out. There is a price. A retina packed for dim light is packed with rods, the cells that catch faint light, and rods do not read color or fine detail. A cat sees a duller, blurrier world than you do. It gained the night and gave up the sharpness. Now the ears. Each ear is a cup of skin and cartilage moved by around thirty muscles, and each one swivels on its own to aim at a sound. A cat hears far higher notes than we do, up to about 64,000 vibrations a second. That is not a random number. It is roughly the pitch of a mouse. Mice call to each other in squeaks too high for human ears, and the cat has spent millions of years listening in on a private conversation. Then the whiskers finish the job. Up close, where the eyes go soft, whiskers read the shape of a mouse in the dark by the air moving around it.

it packed its retina with rods for dim light, so it lost color and fine detail
it matches the pitch of a mouse, so the hearing evolved to catch mouse squeaks

blocks.prompt: The Cat That Always Lands Feet First
blocks.text: Drop a wrench and it tumbles. Drop a cat from the same height and it arrives on its feet, calm, as if the whole thing had been its idea. For a long time this looked like a violation of physics. The problem is a real one. A body that starts a fall without spinning has no angular momentum, and nothing in midair can hand it any. There is no floor to push against, no wall, nothing but air. By the strict rule, a cat that begins a fall upside down should stay upside down. The cat gets around the rule instead of breaking it. In 1894 a French scientist named Etienne Jules Marey photographed a falling cat sixty times a second and finally saw the trick. The cat bends sharply at the waist, folding into two halves that can turn separately. It pulls its front legs in tight and throws its back legs out wide. A tucked half spins easily; a spread half resists. So the front end whips around while the back end barely moves. Then the cat swaps: back legs in, front legs out, and now the rear catches up to the front. Two half turns, and the whole animal has rotated without ever gaining any net spin. The books balance. Physics never noticed. The equipment behind this is worth knowing. In the inner ear sits the vestibular system, which tells the cat instantly which way is down. Its skeleton is unusually forgiving: around 230 bones, a spine with loose, flexible joints, and a collarbone that floats free in muscle instead of bolting to the shoulder. That floating collarbone is why a cat can pour itself through a gap barely wider than its head. One more thing. A falling cat that spreads out reaches a top speed of roughly 60 miles an hour, about half what a falling person reaches, because a cat is light for its surface area and the air has more to push on. Landing feet first is only half the story. The other half is that a cat is simply harder for gravity to hurry.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Felis catus, descended from the African wildcat
Domesticated itself around 10,000 years ago
A cat was buried beside a person on Cyprus 9,500 years ago
Barely changed from its wild ancestor
Hearing reaches about 64,000 vibrations a second
Now on every continent except Antarctica

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Domesticated Itself
blocks.text: Every other domestic animal has the same origin story. People wanted something, went out and got it, and bred it until it was useful. The dog, the cow, the sheep, the horse: all of them were taken. The cat walked in on its own. About 10,000 years ago, in the Fertile Crescent, people stopped following their food and started growing it. Farming produced something the world had never seen before: a pile. Grain in one place, in quantity, sitting still. Mice found the pile almost immediately. And a small, striped, short-tempered predator called the African wildcat found the mice. Nobody recruited it. The cats that could tolerate being near people ate well and raised more kittens. The cats that could not stayed in the hills. Over many generations the tolerant ones changed slightly, mostly in temperament, and became a separate thing. Biologists call this the commensal pathway, from a Latin phrase meaning sharing a table. The cat was not domesticated so much as it accepted a job offer and negotiated its own hours. The oldest hard evidence is a grave. On the island of Cyprus, at a site called Shillourokambos, archaeologists uncovered a human burial about 9,500 years old with a cat laid carefully beside it, roughly sixteen inches away, facing the same direction. What makes the grave remarkable is the geography. Cyprus has no native wildcats. Someone put that animal on a boat and carried it across open sea, which means that by then the relationship was already worth the trouble. From there the cat sailed everywhere. Egypt made it sacred and gave it a goddess, Bastet. Roman ships carried it along trade routes. Later ships carried it to islands that had never held a land predator of any kind. And that is where the story stops being charming. Compare a cat to a dog and the difference is stark. Ten thousand years of dog breeding produced the Chihuahua and the Great Dane. Ten thousand years of cats produced a slightly friendlier African wildcat. Genetically and physically, the house cat is nearly its wild ancestor with the volume turned down. Its eyes, its ears, its claws, its reflexes are the equipment we hired it for, and none of it was ever switched off. A well fed cat still hunts. Hunger was never the trigger. The bill for that is enormous. One widely cited study estimated that free ranging cats in the United States kill somewhere between 1.3 and 4.0 billion birds a year, and several times that many small mammals. On islands, where the local birds evolved with no ground predators and no instinct to fear one, cats have helped push dozens of species out of existence entirely. It is tempting to be angry at the cat. That would be a mistake, and it would also be a dodge. The cat is doing the exact thing it has done for 10,000 years, the thing we valued it for, the thing we shipped it around the planet to do. It has not changed. Our accounting has. We put a wild predator on every continent except one, called it a pet, and are now surprised to find that it hunts.
